intro: Bengaluru, long known as Bangalore, is the garden city of southern India, its avenues and compounds shaded by trees planted since the colonial era. Readers have sent us two of its rain trees: one in the grounds of the National Gallery of Modern Art, its dark limbs fanning out over the lawn in a crown as wide as the building beside it, and one in a small garden in Cooke Town whose huge limbs bend low over the path.
meta_description: Two great rain trees in Bengaluru sent by readers, at the National Gallery of Modern Art and in a Cooke Town garden: where they stand and what we know.

trees.name: The Rain Tree of the National Gallery of Modern Art

location.address: National Gallery of Modern Art, Palace Road, Bengaluru

trees.story:
A reader sent us this rain tree from the garden of the National Gallery of Modern Art in Bengaluru and named it simply "Rain tree, National Gallery of Modern Art."

The photograph shows why it earned a place. A thick, deeply ridged trunk rises only a short way before it divides into a dozen long limbs that fan upward and outward, spreading so far that the crown seems to fill the whole sky above the lawn. The branches are dark and gnarled and stay bare of leaf for a long stretch before they break into fine green foliage high overhead. Rain trees, Samanea saman, came to India from tropical America and have been planted along the avenues and in the gardens of old Bengaluru for generations, and the finest of them take exactly this umbrella shape.

The reader gave no age or girth, and we have none to offer from a source. If you know when this tree was planted, or the gallery's own story of it, tell us here and we will add it.

Stand under the crown and look up through the limbs to see how far they reach.

trees.name: The Rain Tree of Cooke Town
trees.age_estimate: about 60 years, by a reader's estimate

trees.how_to_recognise: In a small garden of palms and shrubs off High Street: a massive dark trunk with a stone bench at its foot, sending out several huge limbs that bend sideways and then turn upward, one of them crossing low over the path.
trees.access: In a small garden with benches off High Street, Cooke Town, where the reader photographed it. We have not confirmed the garden's opening hours.
trees.story:
A reader in Cooke Town, in the east of Bengaluru, sent us this rain tree from a small garden off High Street, and the photograph is mostly limb.

The trunk is massive and dark, its bark broken into small rough plates, and a stone bench sits at its foot as if the garden had been laid out around it. A little way up the tree gives up on growing straight. Huge limbs, each as thick as an ordinary tree, swing out sideways, kink, and turn upward again, one of them crossing low over the path so that anyone walking through ducks beneath it. Above, the fine feathery leaves of a rain tree make a high green roof, and under it the garden has filled with palms and shrubs that thrive in the shade.

Rain trees came to Bengaluru from tropical America and became one of the trees that made it the garden city, prized for the wide shade they cast. The reader puts this one at about 60 years old and five metres round. Those figures are theirs, not a measurement we have seen.

Sit on the bench at the foot of the trunk and look up along the low limb.
